analysis.one_liner: Authorizes Pentagon programs for the year, from weapons purchases to military family benefits.
analysis.headline: The House passed the FY2023 defense authorization 329-101 on July 14, 2022, but the Senate never took an up-or-down vote and the bill died when the Congress ended in January 2023.
analysis.plain_summary: This is the annual defense bill, which authorizes what the Department of Defense can spend and do in the coming fiscal year. It authorizes buying ships, aircraft, and helicopters, sets troop levels, and carries hundreds of separate provisions on personnel policy, military justice, and the military's environmental record. It also raises the minimum wage for workers on federal contracts in statute, restricts PFAS chemicals in military firefighting gear, and orders the defueling of the Red Hill fuel facility that contaminated drinking water in Hawaii.
analysis.who_benefits: Service members and military families gain pay and benefit changes: an inflation bonus, help with child care and spouse relicensing costs, reduced out-of-pocket uniform costs, and temporary elimination of cost-sharing for contraceptives under TRICARE. Communities near military installations gain from bans on buying PFAS-containing firefighting equipment and the ordered defueling of the Red Hill fuel facility. Defense contractors gain authorized purchases of destroyers, aircraft, and helicopters, plus prohibitions that keep the Pentagon from retiring certain planes and ships. Workers on federal contracts gain a congressionally enacted higher minimum wage that an executive order alone could not guarantee.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Military members, families, communities near bases, defense contractors

how_it_helps.text: The bill provides statutory authority for the 2021 executive order raising the minimum wage for federal contractor employees, making the raise a matter of law rather than a policy a future administration could revoke.
It orders the defueling of the Red Hill Bulk Fuel Storage Facility in Hawaii, which leaked fuel into the aquifer serving Oahu, and requires tracking of health effects from the leaks.

It directs the Defense Department toward phasing out PFAS: it prohibits buying firefighting equipment containing the chemicals, offers prizes for non-PFAS turnout gear, and sets standards for cleaning up PFAS contamination at installations.
It temporarily bars TRICARE health programs from imposing cost-sharing for prescription contraceptives and related services.

It adds personnel and family provisions, including reduced out-of-pocket uniform costs, child care reimbursement during moves, spouse relicensing reimbursements, an inflation bonus for troops, and independent investigation and prosecution of sexual harassment and sex-related offenses.
It bars regulators from penalizing banks solely for serving state-legal cannabis businesses, and bars excluding veterans from federal jobs solely because they used cannabis.

analysis.who_pays: Taxpayers fund the entire authorization. Part of the cost goes to platforms and production lines Congress protected from retirement even where the Pentagon wanted to shrink them, such as B-1 bomber squadrons, littoral combat ships, and the HH-60W helicopter line.

drawbacks.text: The bill repeatedly bars the Defense Department from retiring aircraft and ships or ending production lines — including HH-60W helicopters, B-1 bomber squadrons, littoral combat ships, and C-40 aircraft — locking in spending on equipment the military's own reviews favored shedding.
It authorizes very large annual spending on procurement, research, and personnel; the money must still be appropriated each year, and it comes on top of competing demands on the federal budget.

It carries many provisions unrelated to defense, from establishing the San Gabriel National Recreation Area to cannabis banking protections and federal data standards, attached to a bill that passes because failing to fund the military is not an option.
It temporarily suspends the COVID-19 vaccine mandate for Department of Defense contractors, a policy change its supporters did not seek.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill's personnel, family, and environmental provisions are real gains for a specific and often overlooked group of working people — military families and communities near bases — and the contractor minimum wage statute is a durable labor win. But the bill is primarily a vehicle for the annual defense budget, and a number of its provisions push in the opposite direction, protecting weapons programs and production lines the Pentagon itself wanted to cut. The net effect for ordinary taxpayers depends on how much of the authorized spending you consider necessary for national defense; the parts that lock in unwanted programs are hard to defend on the merits.

outcome.mechanism: It passed the House with a strong bipartisan vote, sat on the Senate calendar all summer, was laid before the Senate once in October, and never got a Senate vote before the Congress ended in January 2023.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced May 27, 2022, and referred to the House Armed Services Committee.
The committee reported it after amendment on a 57-1 vote, and it was placed on the Union Calendar.
The House passed it on July 14, 2022, by a vote of 329-101 (Roll no. 350).
The vote was bipartisan: 180 of 220 House Democrats and 149 of 211 House Republicans voted yes; 39 Democrats and 62 Republicans voted no.
The Senate received the bill July 28, 2022, and placed it on the Senate Legislative Calendar on August 3.
The measure was laid before the Senate on October 11, 2022, but no vote on passage is recorded; the 117th Congress ended January 3, 2023, without Senate action on this version.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: No one gained this House version's provisions, because it never became law. Defense funding itself was not at risk — Congress authorizes defense spending every year and carried the FY2023 work into other legislation — so the practical losers were the military families, base communities, and contractor workers counting on this version's specific provisions, who had to wait for the next vehicle. The members who voted against it succeeded in keeping this version from taking effect.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: House no-voters; defense work continued in later bills

industries.industry: Defense contractors (shipbuilders, aircraft and helicopter manufacturers)
industries.note: The bill authorizes purchases of destroyers, aircraft, and helicopters and bars the Pentagon from retiring certain planes and ships or terminating the HH-60W production line, locking in orders and production lines even where the military sought to shrink them. Contractors supply real capability, but these lock-ins are paid for by taxpayers regardless of military judgment.

industries.industry: Firefighting foam and gear manufacturers using PFAS
industries.note: The bill bans Defense Department purchases of firefighting equipment containing PFAS and funds prizes for PFAS-free turnout gear, cutting off a customer for these chemicals in the name of community and service member health.
The bill bars federal regulators from penalizing banks solely for providing services to state-legal cannabis businesses, reducing the risk that legal businesses lose banking access.

The bill writes the higher federal contractor minimum wage into statute, raising contractors' wage costs while guaranteeing pay for their workers in a way an executive order could not; it also temporarily suspends the COVID-19 vaccine mandate for defense contractors.
